en: Taal Volcano erupts when magma from deep underground rises through a volcanic vent, releasing immense pressure and expelling ash and lava.
Water in the Pasig River flows into Manila Bay because gravity pulls it from the higher elevation of Laguna de Bay down to sea level.
The Amihan brings cool, dry weather to the Philippines because high-pressure systems over Siberia push cold air southward across the Asian continent.
The Philippine archipelago formed because the collision of the Eurasian and Philippine Sea tectonic plates uplifted the ocean floor, creating thousands of islands.
Philippine tarsiers survive in Bohol because the island's isolated rainforest environment protected them from large predators, allowing their special nighttime traits to evolve.
Mount Pulag experiences freezing temperatures and frost because its high elevation causes the surrounding air to expand and cool rapidly as it rises.
The Chico River carved deep valleys in the Cordilleras because flowing water slowly eroded and washed away the soft rock and soil over thousands of years.
Tubbataha Reef thrives because the clear, warm, shallow waters of the Sulu Sea allow sunlight to reach coral polyps, enabling them to build massive limestone structures.
Laguna de Bay formed because ancient volcanic eruptions and shifting earth plates blocked the natural drainage of the surrounding lowlands, trapping water to create a massive basin.
The Sierra Madre mountains protect Luzon from typhoons because their massive, dense forests absorb heavy rainfall and physically block strong winds before they reach inland areas.
The Tiwi geothermal plant generates electricity because underground magma heats water into steam, which is piped to the surface to spin turbines and produce power.
The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River formed because slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolved the thick limestone bedrock of St. Paul Mountain, carving a massive underground cave system.
